![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14149458/assets/e2ded513c72c8029b7d2909d2e3b37cbd659c4ba60a7be72c81379626a7a1234.png)

Consider the region $D$ shown above. If $R=[-1,2]\times [-1,3],$ and

$$
{∬}_{D}{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

which of the following could be the definition of $f(x,y)?$

I. $\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y, & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D\end{aligned}$

II. $\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y, & (x,y)\in R∖D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in D\end{aligned}$

III. $\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y, & (x,y)\in R \\ 0, & (x,y)\notin R\end{aligned}$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's draw our region $D$ and rectangle $R:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14149458/assets/77c8e1b1aacd29c6d69aa3c641c1641f43ff2aa1467dc713d417641f8b76b066.png)

Notice that the rectangle $R$ contains the region $D$ completely. 

Now, if we define $f(x,y)$ to be equal ${e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ on $D$ and to be equal $0$ outside $D,$ we obtain

$$
{∬}_{D}{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given functions.

- We cannot use functions II and III. Both of these functions are not identically zero for all points in $R\,∖D.$ For example, $(x,y)=(2,3)\in R\,∖\,D,$ but the functions are nonzero at this point.

- Function I equals ${e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ on $D$ and equals $0$ outside $D.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
